about: Lesson content for learn.html. Every item has thai, roman and mean; example sentences are optional. 'say' (optional) is what the Listen button speaks when it should differ from 'thai'. Progress is saved by the thai text, so changing it resets that item's progress.

romanization.intro: Romanization is only a guide: listen to the voice and copy it. Long vowels are written twice (aa, ii, uu). The accent shows the tone, and no accent means mid tone.

keys.say: no puff of air (as in skin, spin, stop)
with a puff of air. ph is never f, th is never the th in ‘the’

tones.intro: Thai has five tones. The tone is part of the word: the same sound with a different tone is a different word. Listen to each tone, then to the sets of words below that differ only by tone.

list.name: Mid
list.thai: เสียงสามัญ
list.how: Level, in the middle of your normal voice.

list.name: Low
list.how: Level and low, a little below your normal voice.

list.name: Falling
list.how: Starts high and drops, like a firm ‘No!’.

list.name: High
list.how: High and rising a little, a bit tense.

list.name: Rising
list.thai: เสียงจัตวา
list.how: Dips, then rises, like a surprised ‘Really?’.

marks.intro: There are four tone marks, written above the consonant. A mark does not always give the tone of its name: the result depends on the consonant class (see Consonants).

sets.title: The “mai” set
sets.note: Five everyday words that differ only by tone. ไม้ is written with a short vowel but said long.

example.thai: ไม้ใหม่ไม่ไหม้ไหม
example.mean: New wood doesn’t burn, does it? (a classic tone twister)

sets.title: The “khaa” set
sets.note: The same syllable with five tones. Notice how ข (high class) and ค (low class) give different tones with the same mark.

sets.title: The “bpaa” set
sets.note: ป is a middle-class consonant, the only class that normally uses all four tone marks.

items.mean: dad (informal); slang for a generous older man
